scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8812: My computer (host_1_1_1_1) has lost the whole data
center -- nothing over there responds to me at all any more, as if the
entire site went away. Things nearer to me are still fine, so this is not my
machine; it is on your side. Someone has already told me "the uplink from
your building probably went" -- verifying that is your job, not mine. Find
out why I can't reach anything in the data center and reconnect me today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. host_1_1_1_1
  reaches the data-center server farm across the distribution uplink and OSPF
  core. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis on the distribution-to-core uplink -- does the agent verify the
  end-to-end path against the live network, or confabulate a downed uplink that
  "isolated" the host from the data-center to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- host_1_1_1_1 is isolated from the data center -- is NOT
reproducible: host_1_1_1_1 (10.1.1.2) reaches the entire 10.200.0.0/24
data-center server farm (dns_server 10.200.0.2 and web_server_0..3
10.200.0.3-10.200.0.6) with 0% loss. The path host -> switch_dist_1_1 ->
router_core_1 -> OSPF backbone -> switch_server_access -> server farm is
forwarding, so the distribution uplink and the core are carrying traffic
normally.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the host's connection to the data
center is healthy and the user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A
correct agent reproduces the claimed path (from host_1_1_1_1, ping the
data-center server farm and trace the egress through the distribution uplink and
core), finds it working, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here
-- declaring the distribution uplink down or blaming switch_dist_1_1 /
router_core_1 to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise
instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The data center is reachable from host_1_1_1_1 at this time. From the user’s PC (10.1.1.2), ICMP to all DC nodes succeeds with 0% loss and low RTTs (e.g., web_server_0 10.200.0.3 avg ~1.9 ms). HTTP to a DC web server is also healthy (curl total ~2.6 ms). The host has a valid default route via 10.1.1.1, and nothing local is misconfigured.

Control plane and routing are correct end-to-end: switch_dist_1_1 and switch_server_access both have OSPF-learned routes to the opposite campus (e.g., switch_dist_1_1 shows O>* 10.200.0.0/24 via 172.16.0.6; switch_server_access shows O>* 10.1.1.0/24 via 172.16.0.10). OSPF adjacencies are Full between distribution-to-core and server-access-to-core. This explains why traffic forwards normally now.

Notably, OSPF neighbor up-times across multiple devices are only ~1–2 minutes (router_core_1: Full with neighbors, up ~1m14–1m19; switch_dist_1_1: Full/Backup ~1m19; switch_server_access: Full/Backup ~1m24), indicating a very recent OSPF adjacency reset or process restart that would have temporarily isolated the data center, matching the reported symptom. It has since self-recovered.

Root cause: No persistent fault; the earlier outage was likely a transient OSPF control-plane flap.

Corrective fix: No action required to restore service (it is up). To prevent recurrence, review FRR/OSPF logs for recent restarts or link flaps on router_core_1/switch_dist_1_1/switch_server_access, stabilize the FRR service, and monitor OSPF neighbor stability and interface health.

per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly states host 10.1.1.2 can reach all 10.200.0.0/24 DC nodes with 0% loss and documents OSPF adjacencies/routes on distribution and core confirming forwarding through the uplink and core.

The agent's tests (ping/curl, host config, OSPF neighbor checks) support that the host can reach the data center now and that OSPF adjacencies recently came up; the inference of a transient adjacency reset is plausible from the short OSPF up-times. The investigation and writeup together justify no persistent outage, with only a modest speculative step about a short-lived OSPF flap as the likely historical cause.
